newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FEATURE - South Asian tea industry set for boom.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - South Asian tea industry set for boom.

text.p: The South Asian tea industry is poised for a good year in 1996, with prices climbing despite record high crops, brokers and analysts say.

Sri Lanka, India and Bangladesh, which form the South Asian tea triangle, all forecast bumper harvests. But voracious global demand, particularly from the Commonwealth of Independent States, is driving tea prices higher, they said.
"I reckon 1996 production will once again be an all time high," said Rohan Iddawela of Colombo brokers Forbes & Walker. "It is a good time for the Sri Lankan producer."
Sri Lanka, the world's biggest tea exporter, posted a record production of 245.9 million kg (542.1 million lb) in 1995.

India, one of the world's biggest tea producers and consumers, expects a production of 775 million kg (1.709 billion lb) in 1996, up from 754 million (1,662 lb) a year earlier, according to R. K. Krishna Kumar, chairman of India's Consultative Committee of Plantation Associations.
"The crop is up. The outlook is bright," Kumar said.
He said the Indian tea industry was optimistic about increasing the annual production to 1.08 billion kg (2.381 billion lb) by 2006, of which 255 million kg (562.2 million lb) would be for export.
RUSSIA BUYING MORE TEA

"Russia is currently buying more tea from Sri Lanka despite an increase in their prices because it is offering longer term credit," said V. Ramaswamy, of Indian tea auctioners Carritt Moran. "This particularly affects the south Indian market."

About 75 percent of India's tea is produced in the northeastern states of Assam, Meghalaya and Tripura, along with Darjeeling in West Bengal, with the remainder grown in the southern states of Kerala, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
Bangladesh also expects a higher tea output at 54 million kg (119 million lb) this year against 47.47 million (104.7 million lb) in 1995, brokers said.
They said markets for tea have been rallying on heavy buying ahead of the northern hemisphere's winter.

Sri Lanka, which exported a record 240 million kg (529.1 million lb) in 1995, filling about 20 percent of the world's demand, shipped 113.9 million kg (251.1 million lb) in the first six months of this year ahead of the heavy buying season, they said.
FOREIGN SALES COUPLED WITH HIGH PRICES

These high foreign sales have been coupled with high prices. The national average price for a kilogramme (2.2 lb) of Sri Lankan tea at the end of July was 102.94 rupees ($1.87), compared with the average of 62.60 rupees a year earlier.
"The main reason for the high average in 1996 is the extremely satisfactory market conditions that prevailed for low grown teas," said Forbes & Walker's Iddawela.

Sri Lanka's distinctive low growns, accounting for about half the country's tea crop, stayed above a 100-rupee average in the first six months of 1996, as newcomers in the CIS and traditional Middle Eastern buyers competed for the available quantities.
Demand for Sri Lankan tea has soared since the collapse of the former Soviet Union, which unleashed competition among the new independent states of the CIS.
Russia and other CIS states, which bought 40.4 million kg (89.07 million lb) of Sri Lanka tea last year, imported 21.4 million kg (47.18 million lb) in the first half of 1996.

Traders said the CIS market had become so lucrative that a lot of the tea bought by Turkey, the second largest importer of Sri Lankan tea, was re-exported north to the CIS. Turkey took 15.6 million kg (34.39 million lb) in the first six months of this year, against only 3.5 million (7.716 million lb) during the same 1995 period.
Both India and Bangladesh were seeking more business from Pakistan, the world's second largest importer.
"India is looking into the Pakistan market. We are hopeful of striking a deal with Pakistani importers soon," said Ramaswamy of Carritt Moran.
Pakistan, traditionally the biggest buyer of Bangladeshi teas, is coming back after being a poor buyer in 1995, when it bought only 2.57 million kg (5.666 million lb).

Poland topped Bangladesh's buyers' list last year, taking 11.64 million kg (25.66 million lb), followed by Sudan's 4.7 million (10.36 million lb) and Russia's 4.34 million (9.568 million lb). Other buyers included Afghanistan, Britain, Japan, Jordan, Oman, and the United Arab Emirates.
Officials of Bangladesh's National Brokers Ltd said Pakistan and Iran had been buying the bulk of the tea offered in the past few weekly auctions for unspecified reasons.
"This has triggered a rush of buying by other importers, who fear tea prices will move up," one official said.
The average tea price in the Bangladesh auction in late August was 44.89 taka ($1.07) per kg, compared with 40.0 taka in June.
Industry officials said foreign buyers were interested in Bangladeshi low grade teas for blending with better quality leaves from other countries.
India has also signed deals to export four million kg (8.818 million lb) of tea to Iran in the year to next April, said D. K. Ghosh, chairman of the Calcutta Tea Traders' Association.

"Iran has floated tenders for buying 6,000 tonnes of tea and we are hoping to bag contracts for the remaining quantity too," Ghosh said, adding that two thirds of the volume had been signed by five Indian exporters in Teheran with Iran's State Tea Organisation.
Iran had been a traditional buyer of Indian tea with annual imports of over 15,000 tonnes a year. But it stopped buying Indian tea in 1992 because of a severe foreign exchange crunch, he said.
"The contracts are very significant for the Indian tea industry as we have regained a lost market," Ghosh said.
($1=55 Sri Lankan rupee, $1=42 taka, $1=36 Indian rupee)
